title: Rasova steps down from SODELPA GS role - Fiji Sun
content: "I resigned because I was not in a position to be a candidate," Mr Rasova said. Former Social Democratic Liberal Party general secretary Simione Rasova Simione Rasova has re­signed as general sec­retary of the Social Democratic Liberal Party (SODELPA), with party leader Aseri Radrodro confirming the resignation. Mr Rasova's resignation comes amid concerns over an upcoming court case and its impli­cations for the party's prepa­rations for the 2026 General Election. Mr Radrodro said Mr Rasova had formally tendered his resignation to the SODELPA president "I can confirm Mr Rasova has tendered his resignation as GS to the party president of SODELPA citing his upcoming court case and its implications on the party preparations to the general election," Mr Radrodro said. Mr Rasova confirmed he re­signed last Friday but said his departure from the general secretary's position would not mean an end to his support for SODELPA. "I resigned because I was not in a position to be a candidate," Mr Rasova said. He will continue to support the party and aid its candidates as SODELPA prepares for the elec-tion. The resignation comes less than a year after Mr Rasova was elected general secretary on September 6, 2025, during a man­agement board meeting at the Tamavua Village Hall in Suva. He had signed a two-year term with the responsibility of help­ing rebuild the party's struc­tures ahead of the election.

title: This 300-HP Lexus Sleeper Matched BMW Muscle Without The German Repair Bills - HotCars
content: By the late 1990s, the luxury sports sedan had evolved into one of the automotive industry's fiercest battlegrounds. Premium automakers were no longer competing solely on refinement, prestige, or comfort—straight-line performance had become just as important. Yet impressive acceleration figures alone weren't enough to win enthusiast approval. Reputation increasingly depended on something less tangible: how a car made its driver feel. Amid that landscape, one Japanese luxury sedan quietly produced performance numbers comparable to the benchmark BMW 540i, yet never earned the same reputation. Its greatest disadvantage wasn't found beneath the hood or within its chassis, but somewhere far less mechanical. By the time the E39-generation BMW 540i arrived,     BMW had already established itself as the benchmark for building sports sedans that balanced luxury with genuine driver involvement. The 540i refined that formula further by combining a smooth, naturally aspirated V8 with a chassis that felt equally comfortable on a winding back road and a long-distance highway journey. It wasn't the fastest executive sedan of its era, nor the most powerful, but it delivered an experience that felt complete in a way few rivals managed. Much of that reputation stemmed from BMW's decision to offer the 540i with a six-speed manual transmission. At a time when luxury manufacturers were increasingly steering buyers toward sophisticated automatic gearboxes, BMW continued to cater to enthusiasts who valued direct mechanical engagement above outright convenience. The manual-equipped 540i became more than just another drivetrain option—it became central to the car's identity and helped cement its status as the driver's choice within the segment. That timing proved significant because enthusiast culture increasingly equated three pedals with authenticity. Automotive publications praised manual transmissions for the greater sense of involvement they provided, while buyers often viewed them as proof that a manufacturer genuinely prioritized the driving experience. Automatic transmissions had become smoother, more intelligent, and, in many situations, equally capable, but public perception hadn't evolved at the same pace. As a result, any rival hoping to challenge the BMW faced an obstacle extending well beyond measurable performance. Matching its acceleration or handling would not automatically earn the same respect if enthusiasts believed the driving experience itself was compromised. It was against this backdrop that another luxury manufacturer quietly pursued a fundamentally different vision for the modern performance sedan. While much of the segment increasingly embraced the formula that had made German performance sedans so desirable, one manufacturer chose not to chase driver involvement in exactly the same way. Instead of building a car that demanded constant interaction, its engineers focused on delivering effortless performance, exceptional refinement, and the kind of long-term durability that had already become a defining strength of the brand. The objective wasn't to imitate the benchmark—it was to prove there was another path to building a genuinely capable luxury performance sedan. That philosophy shaped the development of a new rear-wheel-drive executive sedan that represented a significant departure from its predecessor. Engineers strengthened the chassis, refined the suspension, sharpened steering response, and improved overall body control, but resisted sacrificing ride quality simply to create a harsher, more aggressive character. The goal remained balance rather than extremity, ensuring the car retained the comfort expected of a premium luxury sedan while becoming noticeably more rewarding to drive. The same thinking extended beneath the hood. Rather than chasing peak horsepower figures alone, engineers concentrated on creating a V8 that delivered broad, effortless torque, exceptional smoothness, and dependable performance over hundreds of thousands of miles. Variable Valve Timing with intelligence (VVT-i) broadened the engine's operating range, while careful calibration prioritized immediate real-world response instead of requiring constant high-rev driving to access meaningful performance. The result reflected an engineering philosophy that valued usable speed over dramatic theater. That approach ultimately produced a luxury sedan capable of matching the segment's established benchmark where objective performance was concerned—even if it arrived there through an entirely different philosophy. That sedan was the Lexus GS 400, introduced as the flagship performance model of the second-generation GS lineup. Rather than attempting to replicate BMW's character, Lexus developed the GS 400 to demonstrate that effortless refinement and genuine performance could coexist without compromise. It wasn't designed to become a track-focused sports sedan or a luxury car with a larger engine. Instead, it embodied Lexus's belief that engineering sophistication could deliver competitive performance while remaining unmistakably Lexus. Power came from a revised 4.0-liter 1UZ-FE V8 equipped with VVT-i, producing 300 horsepower and 310 lb-ft of torque. Paired exclusively with a five-speed electronically controlled automatic transmission driving the rear wheels, the GS 400 recorded 0–60 mph times ranging from approximately 5.7 to 6.0 seconds in contemporary road tests, depending on the publication. Those figures placed it directly alongside the BMW 540i and Mercedes-Benz E420/E430, proving that Lexus had achieved genuine parity where straight-line performance was concerned. The engine's character mattered just as much as its headline figures. With roughly 80 percent of its peak torque available from just 1,800 rpm, the revised 1UZ-FE delivered immediate, seamless acceleration across almost the entire rev range. Rather than encouraging drivers to chase redlines, it produced effortless thrust whether pulling away from traffic lights, merging onto a highway, or overtaking slower vehicles. That broad torque delivery perfectly reflected Lexus' grand touring philosophy, making the GS 400 feel consistently responsive without demanding constant driver effort. The industry's recognition of the 1UZ-FE reinforced that engineering achievement. The V8 earned repeated praise for combining refinement, performance, and durability, including recognition through Ward's 10 Best Engines program during the GS 400's production period. It demonstrated that Lexus hadn't simply built a reliable luxury engine—it had created one of the most sophisticated V8 powerplants of its era. On paper and on the road, the GS 400 had achieved exactly what it set out to do: produce performance capable of running with the BMW 540i through engineering rather than imitation. Despite matching the     BMW 540i in outright performance, the GS 400 never achieved the same standing among driving enthusiasts. The reason had little to do with horsepower, acceleration, or chassis capability. Instead, it came down to a single product decision that shaped public perception from the moment the car arrived in showrooms. Unlike the BMW 540i, which offered buyers the option of a six-speed manual transmission, the GS 400 was available exclusively with a five-speed electronically controlled automatic. Lexus engineered the transmission to prioritize smoothness and refinement, while its E-Shift manual mode allowed drivers to select gears sequentially. For everyday driving, it was quick, unobtrusive, and well matched to the V8's broad torque curve. But to enthusiasts accustomed to equating manual gearboxes with driver involvement, it wasn't enough. Period road tests reflected that contrast. Reviewers consistently praised the GS 400's composure, effortless power delivery, and remarkable refinement, often acknowledging that it could match or closely trail the BMW in objective performance testing. Yet when discussions turned to driver engagement, the conversation almost inevitably returned to the BMW's manual transmission. The ability to choose gears manually with a clutch pedal created a stronger emotional connection, even if it offered little measurable advantage in day-to-day performance. That distinction ultimately shaped how both cars were remembered. The BMW became the enthusiast's benchmark because it delivered not only speed, but also a level of interaction that buyers associated with a true driver's car. The Lexus, meanwhile, was viewed as the more mature and refined alternative—a car that achieved similar results through engineering sophistication rather than mechanical theater. In hindsight, its reputation was influenced less by what it could do than by what it chose not to offer. Viewed through a modern lens, the GS 400's philosophy appears surprisingly forward-thinking. Today's high-performance luxury sedans are almost exclusively equipped with sophisticated automatic transmissions, while smooth, effortless torque delivery has become a defining characteristic of the segment. The qualities that once led some enthusiasts to dismiss the Lexus have since become accepted as the industry standard. Its naturally aspirated 1UZ-FE V8 has also earned a reputation for exceptional durability, with numerous examples covering high mileage while retaining the refinement that made the engine so impressive when new. Combined with conservative styling, solid build quality, and a well-balanced rear-wheel-drive platform, the GS 400 has become increasingly appreciated by enthusiasts seeking an understated performance sedan that can still be driven and enjoyed without constant mechanical attention. Perhaps more importantly, time has shifted the conversation away from what the GS 400 lacked and toward what it accomplished. Rather than attempting to imitate BMW's formula, Lexus proved there was another way to build a compelling performance sedan—one that prioritized seamless power delivery, engineering refinement, and everyday usability without sacrificing genuine pace. That philosophy may not have generated the same enthusiast mythology as the manual-equipped 540i, but it produced a car that has aged with remarkable dignity. The GS 400 was never remembered as loudly as its German rival, yet history suggests it deserved greater recognition. It demonstrated that matching the benchmark didn't require copying it, and that intelligent engineering could be just as effective as chasing the traditional enthusiast playbook. Its legacy is therefore defined not by the transmission it never offered, but by how convincingly it proved there was more than one route to building a great V8 sport sedan. title: GS rates may correct on US move to support bonds - BusinessWorld Online
content: RATES of the government securities (GS) to be offered this week may end mixed amid increased volume as the Treasury is set to auction off cash management bills anew, and with the United States’ effort to support long-dated bonds seen to stem the rise in yields. On Monday, the Bureau of the Treasury (BTr) will auction off up to P80 billion in short-term securities. Broken down, it will offer P20 billion in 35-day cash management bills (CMBs). It last sold CMBs on July 20. Meanwhile, it will auction off up to P60 billion in Treasury bills (T-bills). Specifically, the Treasury will look raise P20-25 billion from 91-day papers, P15-20 billion via 182-day securities, and P7-15 billion through 364-day debt. On Tuesday, the government is targeting to borrow P30 billion from reissued seven-year Treasury bonds (T-bonds) with a remaining life of three years and one month. Debt yields could be mixed or slightly lower, tracking movements at the secondary market, after the US Treasury announced they will increase buybacks of long-term US government bonds to help bring down yields after a global rout, Rizal Commercial Banking Corp. Chief Economist Michael L. Ricafort said in a Viber message. This could help reduce borrowing costs around the world, he said. “The government securities (GS) market traded 3 basis points (bps) lower as it tracked US Treasury movements as US Treasury Secretary Bessent announced a surprise increase in long-term bond buybacks. Nonetheless, players used the opportunity to lighten positions,” a trader said in an e-mail. “Price action was generally two-way but offers were noticeably heavy.” As a result, the trader said the reissued bonds to be sold this week could see good demand and fetch rates from 6.775% to 6.8%. At the secondary market on Thursday, yields on the 35- and 91-day tenors rose by 3.56 bps and 5.39 bps week on week to close at 4.7644% and 5.0025%, according to the PHP Bloomberg Valuation Service Reference Rates published on the Philippine Dealing System website. Meanwhile, the 182-day and 364-day T-bills went down by 1.73 bps and 5.78 bps to end at 5.3212% and 5.6593%. For its part, the seven-year bond went up by 3.84 bps to end at 7.2124%, while the three-year tenor, the closest to the remaining life of the bond series on offer on Tuesday, inched up by 1.23 bps to close at 6.6877%. Mr. Ricafort added that inflation concerns could also affect yield movements as the Middle East war continues. Bets on the Bangko Sentral ng Pilipinas’ (BSP) policy move this week and direction moving forward could likewise be on the market’s radar, he said. The government last offered 35-day cash management bills on July 20, where it raised P20 billion as planned at an average rate of 4.816%. The Treasury began offering CMBs again in June for the first time since the pandemic to manage short-term liquidity needs amid elevated interest rates. Meanwhile, last week, the BTr raised P54.8 billion from the T-bills it auctioned off, above the P46 billion on offer as total tenders reached P167.016 billion. This came as the government doubled its acceptance of noncompetitive bids for the six-month and one-year tenors to P12 billion and P5.6 billion, respectively. Broken down, the Treasury borrowed P24 billion as planned via the 91-day T-bills as bids for the tenor reached P42.7 billion. The three-month paper fetched an average rate of 5.008%, up by 1.3 bps from the previous week. Bids accepted had yields from 4.9% to 5.026%. For the 182-day debt, the government raised P21 billion, above the P15-billion plan as tenders hit P84.09 billion. The average yield on the six-month T-bill was at 5.442%, dropping by 10.3 bps from the last auction. Tenders awarded had rates from 5.4% to 5.463%. Lastly, the BTr sold P9.8 billion in 364-day securities, higher than the P7-billion program, as demand for the tenor totaled P40.226 billion. The one-year paper fetched an average rate of 5.613%, declining by 1.8 bps week on week. Accepted yields ranged from 5.595% to 5.633%. Meanwhile, the reissued seven-year T-bonds to be offered on Tuesday were last auctioned off on July 28, where the government raised a total of P40 billion, or P30 billion via the regular auction and P10 billion from a tap facility offering. The papers fetched an average yield of 7.217%, above the 7% coupon rate. The Treasury plans to raise P330 billion from the domestic market this month, or P200 billion via T-bills and P130 billion through T-bonds. The government borrows from local and foreign sources to help finance its budget deficit, which is capped at P1.659 trillion or 5.4% of gross domestic product this year. — Aaron Michael C. Sy

title: A fine of 1.027 billion won has been confirmed for GS Retail, which has passed the burden on supplie.. - 매일경제
content:
A fine of 1.027 billion won has been confirmed for GS Retail, which has passed the burden on suppliers by transferring promotional costs. According to the legal community on the 23rd, the Supreme Court Department 3 (Chief Justice Roh Kyung-pil) recently confirmed its ruling against the plaintiff in a lawsuit filed by GS Retail against the Fair Trade Commission for cancellation, including a corrective order. On January 26, 2022, the FTC imposed a fine of 1.027 billion won along with a correction order and notification order, saying GS Retail violated the Large Distribution Business Act. GS Retail has three major violations of the law. ▲Burden of promotional expenses such as free gift events between January 2015 and November 2018 to the supplier without written agreement (violation of Clause 1 and Clause 2 of Article 11 of the Large Distribution Business Act) ▲Return of many products from April 2017 to October 2019 after receiving only a request for export from the supplier (violation of Clause 1 of Article 10) ▲In January 2018 and June 2020, broadcasters and celebrities belonging to suppliers were required to perform guest or model duties for their home shopping broadcasts without a written agreement on the terms of dispatch (violation of Clause 1 of Article 12). According to the law, large retailers cannot return products purchased directly. The supplier shall voluntarily request a return by attaching objective evidence in writing that the return benefits them directly. This is to prevent large companies from handing over inventory to suppliers. Receiving personnel from suppliers is also prohibited to block 'gapjil'. Only if the terms of dispatch are agreed in writing in advance are limited. GS Retail filed a lawsuit saying it cannot accept the FTC's fine. The FTC disposition had the same effect as the first trial decision, so it was immediately judged by the second trial. At the trial, GS Retail claimed that it was a voluntary return because it received a request for export from suppliers, and that the broadcaster was not a "employee" who was prohibited by law from being dispatched. He also said that even if the law is violated, the FTC's penalty is excessive. The court did not accept it. The second trial court pointed out, "The violation of the ban on product returns is worth about 1.8 billion won, which is by no means small," adding, "There is a high concern that large retailers will use their superior position in the transaction to provide disadvantages to their counterparts by unfairly taking back their products, thereby entrenching abnormal trading practices and hindering fair trading." Considering that the proportion of violations among all events is small, the act of transferring sales promotion costs was also judged not to be excessive by setting the penalty amount at 175 million won. title: LCK Enters Warring States Era, Halting Gen.G's Reign - 조선일보
content: Gen.G secures third straight regular season title but faces T1, Hanwha Lifee in playoffs amid intensified competition LCK (League of Legends Champions Korea) has entered a 'Spring and Autumn Warring States period' after five years. LCK concluded its 2026 regular season on the 23rd and will enter the postseason starting on the 26th. Due to participation in the Aichi-Nagoya Asian Games, the regular season was reduced by one round compared to last year. Gen.G secured the regular league title for the third consecutive year, including the 2024 spring and summer seasons. However, this season's notable trend was that Gen.G, which had established itself as the 'sole powerhouse' in the regular league over the past two years, showed signs of instability in performance from the early stages of the season, leading to a rare intense competition where the top spot was only confirmed in the final match. For the first time in five years since the 2021 summer season, there was no absolute powerhouse dominating the league. Both the 'Legend Group' consisting of the top five teams and the 'Rise Group' made up of the bottom five teams in rounds 3–4 engaged in fierce competition for rankings until the final stages. Gen.G suffered a 1–2 comeback defeat against DiPlus KIA in the final regular season match held on the 22nd. Gen.G took the first set, giving them an advantage in set differential and head-to-head record against second-place Hanwha Lifee Sports. However, they lost the next two sets, securing the top spot somewhat awkwardly. This was a far cry from Gen.G's dominant performance last year, where they suffered only one loss in the single-season format, and two years ago, when they had one loss per season during the split spring and summer seasons. While the team's morale was shaken by late reports of tax evasion allegations surrounding captain 'Ruler' Park Jae-hyuk at the beginning of the season, a more fundamental analysis points to the improved counterplay from opposing teams. Although the current roster has been cohesive for two years, making their teamwork even stronger, opposing teams have accumulated more data and experience to analyze Gen.G. Additionally, the ever-changing meta made it difficult for Gen.G to consistently maintain their previous strengths. The growth of rival teams cannot be overlooked. T1, the eternal rival, showed fluctuations in performance due to fatigue from participating in various international tournaments like MSI and EWC, yet still maintained top-tier competitiveness. Hanwha Lifee Sports, which has formed a three-way power structure with Gen.G and T1 since two years ago, also continued to deliver consistent performance, including an MSI championship, and competed with Gen.G for the top spot until the end. Although Gen.G did not dominate as they did in the past two years, the numerous trials and errors experienced amidst fierce league competition hold significance as they prepare for the playoffs and subsequent international tournaments. Particularly, if Gen.G aims to reach the Worlds (League of Legends World Championship) final and secure the title, which they have yet to achieve since their rebranding, addressing the weaknesses and variables exposed during this season's regular league has become a crucial task. Gen.G has directly advanced to the second round of the playoffs. The winner of the final match between Hanwha Life and T1 on the 23rd will also proceed directly to the second round, while the losing team and fourth-place DiPlus will begin the postseason in the first round of the playoffs. Prior to the playoffs, the 'Play-In' stage will feature KT Rolster, ranked fifth in the Legend Group, facing the top three teams from the Rise Group: Hanjin Brion, BNK Piorx, and Nongshim Red Force. Two teams that survive the Play-In, held from the 26th to the 28th, will join the playoffs.

title: Top Court Upholds Antitrust Fine Against GS Retail - Seoul Economic Daily
content: The Supreme Court has ruled that a fine of about 1 billion won ($720,000) imposed by South Korea's Fair Trade Commission (FTC) on GS Retail, the operator of GS Home Shopping, was justified, finding that the retailer improperly returned goods to suppliers and unfairly passed on promotional costs. The confirmation of the FTC's corrective order and fine is expected to influence trade practices across the country's retail industry. According to legal sources on the 23rd, the third division of the Supreme Court, with Justice Roh Kyung-pil as the presiding judge, upheld the lower court's ruling that had rejected GS Retail's lawsuit against the FTC seeking to overturn the corrective order and other measures. An FTC investigation found that GS Retail violated the Act on Fair Transactions in Large Retail Business by returning about 62,000 items worth around 1.85 billion won ($1.3 million) between April 2017 and October 2019, based only on removal request forms from suppliers. Under the law, a large retailer may not return all or part of goods it has received without justifiable cause. However, in the case of direct purchase transactions, justifiable cause is presumed when a supplier voluntarily requests the return in writing before the return date, attaching objective evidence that the return directly benefits the supplier. The commission also confirmed that GS Retail made suppliers bear the cost of sales promotion events held from January 2015 through 2018 without a prior written agreement on cost-sharing. In addition, from January 2018 to June 2020, it had professional broadcasters, entertainers and others affiliated with suppliers appear as guests or models on home shopping broadcasts without a written agreement on the terms of their dispatch. The FTC ordered GS Retail to pay a fine of 1.027 billion won and issued a corrective order. GS Retail contested the decision and filed a lawsuit. FTC rulings such as sanction decisions carry the same effect as a court's first-instance judgment. As a result, administrative lawsuits concerning fair trade cases and the FTC begin at the Seoul High Court as the first instance, under a two-tier system that then proceeds to the Supreme Court. In May last year, Division 6-2 of the Seoul High Court found the FTC's disposition lawful. The court held that a supplier's request for a return based on documents alone was not enough to accept it as a voluntary request. It cited the fact that GS Retail, during the FTC investigation, had signed a written statement acknowledging that suppliers had borne the cost of sales promotion events without a prior written agreement. The court also considered that 556 of the 562 supplier employees flagged by the FTC were found to have been made to work at GS Retail's own business sites in violation of the Act on Fair Transactions in Large Retail Business. The second-instance court explained that "it is reasonable to view this as conduct in which a large retailer used its superior bargaining position to unfairly impose disadvantages, entrenching abnormal trade practices and posing a significant risk of undermining fair trade," adding that "the FTC's calculation of the fine cannot be seen as an unlawful abuse or deviation of discretion when compared with the gravity of the violations." The Supreme Court upheld the lower court's judgment, finding "no error affecting the ruling, such as misapprehending the facts underlying the calculation of the fine or violating the principles of proportionality and equality." The ruling confirms the fine and corrective order imposed on GS Retail. Analysts say the decision could accelerate efforts to improve unfair practices in the retail industry. title: Supreme Court upholds FTC fine over GS Retail’s unfair costs to SMEs in Korea - CHOSUNBIZ - Chosunbiz
content: Top court backs antitrust order penalizing GS Retail for pushing costs onto small suppliers The Supreme Court ruled that the Korea Fair Trade Commission's corrective order and a 1 billion won penalty surcharge against GS Retail for unfairly shifting expense to suppliers were justified. The Supreme Court's Third Division (presiding Justice Noh Kyung-pil) said on the 23rd that on the 9th it finalized a lower court ruling dismissing GS Retail's suit to cancel the corrective order against the Korea Fair Trade Commission. GS Retail absorbed GS Home Shopping in Jul. 2021. The transaction at issue occurred at GS Home Shopping. Home shopping companies sell products to consumers through broadcasts. When consumers who watch the broadcasted product sales place orders with a home shopping company, the company asks a supplier to deliver the product to the consumer. The home shopping company deducts part of the payment made by the consumer as a sales commission and pays the remainder to the supplier. However, the Korea Communications Commission, to expand sales channels for small and midsize enterprises, evaluates the share of direct purchases of SME products when a home shopping company seeks renewal of its program provider license. Because of this, home shopping companies directly purchase SME products and, when orders arrive, deliver them to consumers. In this case, the inventory burden falls on the home shopping company, not the supplier. From Apr. 2017 to Oct. 2019, GS Retail returned 62,399 directly purchased products from eight SMEs. The purchase amount was 1.85622 billion won. GS Retail did not specifically agree on return conditions when contracting with suppliers. Of the returned products, GS Retail sent back 6,001 items after receiving only a take-out request from suppliers. It returned 56,398 items after receiving a take-out request and documents that included a resale plan. Also, from Jan. 2015 to Nov. 2018, GS Retail conducted sales promotion events—such as free gift promotions and product review events—while selling products supplied by 26 SMEs through broadcasts. At that time, GS Retail made suppliers bear the sales promotion expense. Additionally, from Jan. 2018 to Jun. 2020, while airing 505 broadcasts for products supplied by 144 SMEs, GS Retail had 562 people—supplier-affiliated employees or hired professional broadcasters, entertainers, models, and sales experts—work in its broadcast studio. For these reasons, the Korea Fair Trade Commission (FTC) found that GS Retail violated the Act on Fairness in Large Retail Business and in Jan. 2022 imposed a corrective order along with a 1.027 billion won penalty surcharge. GS Retail filed an administrative suit, arguing the disposition was unjust. In court, GS Retail argued, "Suppliers voluntarily requested returns in writing, attaching objective supporting materials that returns would benefit them." It also said it did not pass on sales promotion expense to suppliers, and that suppliers had their employees appear on home shopping broadcasts for their own benefit. The Seoul High Court dismissed GS Retail's claim. The panel said that in direct-purchase transactions, for returns, suppliers must refund payments already received, incur additional distribution expense, and then resell the products, adding that "suppliers have very little incentive to request returns." It continued, "Based solely on the evidence GS Retail submitted, it is insufficient to find that suppliers voluntarily requested returns." The panel also ruled on the disposition imposing a 1.027 billion won penalty surcharge, saying, "GS Retail's act of prohibiting product returns involves a violation amount of 1.8 billion won, which is by no means small," and "the calculation of the penalty surcharge did not deviate from or abuse discretion compared with the seriousness of the violation." The Supreme Court dismissed GS Retail's appeal, finding the lower court did not misapprehend the legal principles.

The commission found that from April 2017 to October 2019, GS Retail violated Article 10, Paragraph 1 of the Large-scale Retail Business Act by returning a significant number of products to suppliers only after receiving a request for removal, rather than properly documenting the returns process. Furthermore, from January 2015 to November 2018, the company was found to have violated Article 11, Paragraphs 1 and 2 of the same law by carrying out promotional events, such as offering gifts, and shifting the associated costs to suppliers without any prior written agreement on cost sharing. Additionally, from January 2018 to June 2020, GS Retail was judged to have violated Article 12, Paragraph 1 by allowing professional broadcasters and entertainers hired by suppliers to work as broadcast guests and models without a written agreement on dispatch conditions. The key points of contention were whether the request forms or official documents obtained by GS Retail from suppliers constituted objective supporting evidence for the legitimacy of the returns. It was also disputed whether guests employed by suppliers who appeared on GS Home Shopping broadcasts qualified as employees under the law, and whether such broadcast appearances could be considered as labor performed by dispatched employees. Furthermore, there was debate over whether the calculation of the penalty exceeded the Fair Trade Commission's discretionary authority. The appellate court ruled against GS Retail. It found that merely requesting product returns based on a removal request form was insufficient to recognize the voluntary nature of the suppliers' requests for return. Of the 562 employees mentioned by the Fair Trade Commission as working for the suppliers, it determined that 556 were recognized as having worked at the business location in violation of Article 12 of the Large-scale Retail Business Act. The court also found no illegality in the calculation of the penalty. It noted that the amount involved in the violation of the product return prohibition was considerable, at around 1.8 billion won, and that a large-scale retailer like GS Retail using its superior transactional position to impose undue disadvantages would risk normalizing abnormal business practices and significantly undermine fair trade. © The Asia Business Daily. title: 2026 Vikings vs. Ravens Preseason Game Observations - Minnesota Vikings
content: MINNEAPOLIS — Waves of reserves competed for roster spots and roles as Minnesota hosted Baltimore in the second preseason game of 2026 to conclude a productive week packed with purple. The Ravens prevailed 13-3 by keeping the Vikings off the score board in three separate quarters and taking advantage of a drive that was extended by a roughing-the-passer penalty in the second half. Vikings Head Coach Kevin O'Connell and Ravens Head Coach Jesse Minter opted to rest starters Saturday after having those groups take the brunt of practice reps on Wednesday and Thursday during joint sessions. J.J. McCarthy opened and experienced a couple different ups and downs, playing only the first quarter behind an offensive line of Henry Byrd, Joe Huber, Michael Jurgens, Vershon Lee and Ryan Van Demark from left tackle to right tackle. The opening possession started at the 12 after a special teams penalty on the opening kickoff. McCarthy's first throw on an out to Myles Price was high and hot. A false start penalty put Minnesota in second-and-15 from the 7, and McCarthy worked his way out of that with back-to-back 8-yard completions to Tai Felton and Price for a fresh set of downs. The run game, however, didn't start as fast as it did in Minnesota's preseason opener. Rookie Demond Claiborne was stuffed for no gain on his first carry and a loss of 3 a play later. The Vikings were unable to convert third-and-13 on a pass to Felton that gained 8. McCarthy's second series featured the highlight of his day but ended with a lowlight. On second-and-7, he navigated through the pocket, evading a rusher and launched a 50-50 ball to Felton, who secured the catch for a gain of 50 to the Baltimore 10-yard line. McCarthy followed by working through the progression over to Claiborne for a catch-and-run of 7. A pass on second-and-goal at the 3 screaming toward Felton (it needed to be a hard throw) was not secured, and a Claiborne run on third down gained nearly 2. Minnesota opted for a shotgun formation pass on fourth down, and McCarthy had Price open but missed him. A little less mustard would have done the trick. The Vikings had two more series with McCarthy at QB. One play after a sack by Mike Green, McCarthy drilled a pass to Jeshaun Jones for a gain of 19 despite taking a hit. It would have converted third-and-14, but Byrd was flagged for holding, creating a third-and-23 on which Claiborne ran for 9 before a punt. The Vikings committed a false start on their fourth possession. McCarthy took a hit for the fourth time but was accurate with a pass to Price on third-and-13, but Chandler Rivers was credited with a pass defensed. McCarthy finished 5-of-10 passing for 81 yards and a 77.5 passer rating before he was replaced by Carson Wentz in the second quarter. View game action photos from the Vikings preseason game vs. the Ravens at U.S. Bank Stadium. Wentz played two series, including a 2-minute drill to close the first half. He picked up third-and-8 during the drive with a 9-yard pass to Dontae Fleming before firing to Jones for a gain of 35. Jones completed the catch despite an initial bobble and contact that sent him to the turf. Vikings Offensive Coordinator Wes Phillips, who called plays the entire game (O'Connell normally does), dialed up a beautiful tight end screen to Gavin Bartholomew. Walter Rouse got down the field from the left guard spot and absolutely pancaked defensive back Amani Oruwariye to spring Bartholomew for a gain of 16. A sack on second-and-8 from the 27 led Minnesota to opt for a 52-yard field goal by Will Reichard to tie the game at halftime. Wentz finished 9-of-11 passing with 92 yards and a passer rating of 101.5. The Vikings continued evaluating veteran punter Johnny Hekker and rookie Brett Thorson, who held for the long field goal by Reichard. Thorson did not hold at Georgia, so this is the first time he's been tasked with that role, by the way. He punted two times for a gross average of 41.5 with a long of 42 (which means his other was 41), pinning Baltimore inside its 20-yard line with both punts. Hekker punted three times for a gross of 165, averaging 55.0 and uncorking a long of 65 to help flip field position when Minnesota was backed up. Many parts of the box score were not too dissimilar, but the turnover margin was Minnesota at minus-2. The Vikings lost a fumble after a short catch on the third play of a possession that spanned the late third quarter and start of the fourth. Baltimore capitalized on getting the ball on the Vikings side of the field and added a field goal to make it 13-3. Max Brosmer was leading the offense down the field in the fourth quarter but a possession that covered 57 yards ended on the 11th play when Brosmer was intercepted by Silas Walters. Brosmer finished 11-for-17 with 98 yards and a passer rating of 55.5. The longest run allowed by the Vikings went for 8 yards on a scramble by QB Joe Fagnano. Minnesota reserve RB Jermar Jefferson produced the game's only run of 10 or more yards when he got loose for a gain of 15. title: Goldman Sachs (GS) Q2 2026 Earnings Preview: $14.47 EPS Expected, OpenAI IPO Candidacy, and the $1,067 Triangle Trigger - TradingKey

Despite normalizing trading conditions, the firm benefits from strong EMEA M&A activity, potential lead roles in the OpenAI IPO, and $70 billion in new asset management mandates. Trading technically within a symmetrical triangle at $1,047, the stock faces a breakout trigger at $1,067. A potential dividend increase to $5.00 signals management’s confidence in sustained cash flow, though market volatility remains a primary risk factor for upcoming quarters. TradingKey - Goldman Sachs Group (NYSE: GS) is set to announce its second-quarter 2026 results ahead of the market open this morning, July 14, 2026. The initial release is at 7:00 AM ET, followed by the conference call at 8:30 AM ET. Prior to the announcement, analysts had projected a Q2 2026 adjusted Earnings Per Share (EPS) of $14.20 to $14.47, or about 32% higher than last year's Q2 figures of $10.91, on total revenues of $15.9 billion to $16.49 billion, compared to $14.58 billion last year. Goldman has surpassed the Zacks Consensus Estimate in each of the past four quarters, boasting an average EPS surprise of 13.10%. Currently, options are betting on an implied move of roughly 4.78% in either direction. The stock is currently trading at $1,047, within a symmetrical triangle and with an RSI approaching 50. A breakout above $1,067 would target $1,096 and $1,123, whereas a breakdown below $1,029 would expose the 200-period EMA at $1,014. The $14.20 to $14.47 EPS range for the second quarter is down sharply from the record of $17.55 EPS reported in the first quarter. First quarter performance saw a sharp spike in total revenues to $17.23 billion from $14.58 billion the year before, an uptick analysts attributed to a rebound in equity trading. The second quarter consensus revenue forecast of $15.9 billion to $16.49 billion is below the $17.23 billion seen in the first quarter, or a sequential drop in total revenues of 7% to 8%, mostly as the trading environment normalizes. The eight-thirty conference call will help investors determine if (1) investment banking fee revenue grew from the first quarter's strong recovery or if it started losing traction; (2) if the Asset & Wealth Management business can continue its first quarter growth of $4.08 billion, which was up 10% over the same period last year; (3) whether equities revenue normalised from Q1’s $5.33 billion toward the $4.0 to $4.5 billion range that would be consistent with a less-volatile Q2 trading environment, and; (4) whether operating expenses as a percentage of revenue declined from Q1’s $10.43 billion, which at 60.5% efficiency ratio left room for improvement. Goldman has beaten Zacks estimates by 13.10% over the past four quarters; a similar upside against a $14.47 EPS consensus puts second quarter adjusted earnings close to $16.36. Three factors ahead of today's release help frame the medium term revenue outlook outside of the second quarter print. Goldman's M&A in EMEA reached its highest point in 19 years in the first half of 2026, accounting for 44% of all deal value in the region, and confirms that Goldman is taking a larger share of M&A deals in the most lucrative deal environment since 2007. Goldman Sachs and Morgan Stanley are among the two leading prospects to manage the anticipated OpenAI Initial Public Offering (IPO), which would be a source of underwriting revenues that would be in excess of any normal quarter's equity underwriting. Goldman's equity underwriting revenues in the first quarter were $535 million; the OpenAI mandate, should it go through as projected, could produce fee revenues that dwarf this quarterly figure, making it the most significant single event to impact Goldman's third or fourth quarter consensus forecasts. Goldman's Verizon and Lockheed Martin Institutional Retirement Plan mandates, totaling some $70 billion, would be the first tangible milestone of the company's 2030 target for $750 billion in asset under management in the AWM business line, set by David Solomon. Recurring, fee-based revenues from stable institutional assets that aren't subject to redemption in volatile markets would serve as the counterbalance to the cyclical revenue model inherent in the investment banking and trading businesses. If, in the coming days, the board of directors confirms that a sufficient capital cushion is available post-second quarter earnings, Goldman Sachs will be increasing its dividend payout from $4.50 per quarter to $5.00 per quarter, an indication that it expects its free cash flow generation to be able to sustain this increased dividend payout indefinitely On the 4H timeframe, Goldman Sachs is at $1,047 in a consolidation near the apex of the symmetrical triangle after declining from the June top of $1,110. title: GS/OS was Apple’s Colorful Desktop That Lived on the Wrong Machine from the 1980s - TechEBlog -
content: Most people who remember personal computers from the late 1980s think first of the Macintosh and its clean black-and-white interface. Apple had already shipped something that looked and behaved a lot like it, only this version ran in color on a machine that still carried the Apple II name. That system was GS/OS, and it arrived in 1988 as the heart of Apple IIGS System Software 4.0. GS/OS was built from the start in 100% 16-bit code for the 65816 CPU inside the IIGS, which was a significant shift from previous versions. Most other software on this computer was still inadequately optimized for 8-bit routines carried over from the previous Apple II generation. The improved code resulted in significantly faster disk access, screen rendering, and program loading. Customers who had upgraded from ProDOS 16 were particularly affected. title: Limited Edition R 1300 GS Adventure Announced For Brazilian Market - Motorcycle.com
content: BMW Motorrad recently celebrate the ten years of production in Manuas, Brazil, by releasing a limited edition R 1300 GS Adventure. Limited to a run of 10 motorcycles, one for each year of Brazilian production, the commemorative model features a unique graphics in green with yellow striping. The bike comes with a top case, featuring the same pattern in black and green on the back. The Manuas factory opened in 2016, producing eight models including the then-new G 310 R. The original production capacity of the factory was 10,000 units a year, but capacity has since grown, with the factory recently producing its 150,000th motorcycle, fittingly, an R 1300 GS Adventure.

title: Is this BMW's new Ténéré beater? - Motorcycle News
content:
BMW have been incredibly busy of late. In the past three months, we’ve seen spyshots of what appears to be a brand-new S1000RR superbike, further images of a monstrous two-litre R20 boxer twin roadster, and the UK public debut of the six-cylinder ‘Vision K18’ concept bike at the Goodwood Festival of Speed. Now though, it seems that the German brand are back for more, with these latest images taken by our keen spy photographer appearing to show a new mid-sized parallel-twin GS model, ready to bridge the gap between the A2-friendly F450GS and larger F800GS and F900GS model variants. Clearly still in the early stages of its development (and unlikely to be seen until at least 2028) the prototype’s styling is a hefty departure from what we’ve come to expect from the German brand in recent years – with the rally-style screen, tall shoulders and upswept exhaust having more than a whiff of Yamaha Ténéré 700 about it. In fact, if it weren’t for the X-style headlight unit – now a staple of modern GS design – you could quite easily mistake it for a KTM, Aprilia, or something Japanese. Exactly what’s powering this bike is currently unknown. Outside of being a parallel-twin configuration, the capacity and origin of the unit remains a mystery – with BMW now heavily intertwined with Indian manufacturing giant TVS, who produce the F450 for the German brand as well as the larger 585cc, 69bhp Norton Atlas family. Clearly it will sit somewhere between the 47bhp output of the F450GS, and 103bhp from the F900GS, but whether it will sit below the 86bhp F800 or simply come in to replace it in the line-up remains to be seen. A look at the side profile reveals a few similarities with both BMW’s existing 895cc unit used in the 800 and 900 flavours, as well as the smaller capacity unit found in the Norton, however neither are identical – suggesting it’ll be a new design for this platform, likely to spawn multiple derivatives. It’ll also likely have a 270-degree firing order, which has become the norm for parallel-twin engines of this capacity class. This is further evidenced by the steel bridge frame holding it in place, which again differs from existing bikes in either range – exposing more of the head of the engine and appearing to hold it as a stressed member behind the chunky radiator. A small bash plate wraps around the base to protect the sump, with hefty ground clearance and 21/18in spoked wheel combo suggesting proper off-road intentions. But what to call it? Well, our sources suggest BMW could be looking to resurrect the F650GS name – last seen in 2013 – however it could also stretch to 700 if it’s destined to go up against the likes of the Ténéré, Aprilia Tuareg 660, Ducati DesertX, and more. In fact, given the current close proximity between the F800 and F900 models, it’s likely that BMW could discontinue the lower model – keeping the F900 to go up against the likes of the Triumph Tiger 900 family, and this new model providing a more all-terrain, A2 restrictable proposition. Away from the engine, the early off-road intentions are clear – with long-travel front suspension, hand guards, chunky foot pegs, and a rider triangle that appears to have been developed with standing in mind. Although partially covered, there’s also clearly room for a pillion, however the upswept exhaust could cause issues for luggage should it remain at such a length and angle. Using the male seen pushing the bike for reference, the seat height also appears to be tall – perhaps in the region of 860-870mm. Under the base of the fairing is a steering damper, with the rear shock mounted at an almost 45-degree angle between the banana-style swing arm and rear of the chassis. At this stage, it’s difficult to tell the level of adjustment available, and given the infancy of the project, the final design settings are likely still yet to come. We’d expect there to be an off-road style front beak to come to complete the look of the front end, and while it’s dressed in Metzeler road tyres here, a slightly knobblier option could also follow, too. MCN approached BMW about the images, however they declined to comment. After a quiet show season in 2025, BMW seem to be cooking up an awful lot of new metal at the moment – ready for a significant revamp across 2027 and 2028. Exactly when or if this model will appear remains to be seen, but MCN will bring you more as soon as it’s available. title: If BMW Brings Back the F 650 GS, It's Reviving the Bike That Made Budget Adventure Riding Mainstream - Top Speed
content: Spy shots published this week show BMW testing an all-new middleweight adventure prototype that appears to slot directly between the F 450 GS and F 900 GS — a gap that has existed in the lineup for years. The prototype rolls on 21-inch front and 18-inch rear cross-spoke wheels, uses a steel bridge frame closely related to the F 900 GS, and carries a parallel-twin engine with visible kinship to the F 450 GS's powerplant. Whether it arrives as an F 600 GS, F 650 GS, or F 700 GS, the nameplate question alone is enough to get adventure riders talking. For many in the community, the F 650 GS badge carries real weight. The F 650 GS Dakar from the early 2000s remains a benchmark for what an accessible, genuinely capable adventure bike can be — the kind of machine that introduced a generation of riders to long-distance dirt travel before the segment exploded into what it is today. BMW returning to that territory, with a modern platform and the resources of the GS family behind it, would be a significant moment for the middleweight adventure market. The prototype is clearly a mix of components drawn from across BMW's existing GS range. The chassis and braking system lean toward the F 900 GS, while the rear shock mounting and swingarm design echo the smaller F 450 GS. Ground clearance looks generous — observers estimate around 230 millimeters (roughly nine inches) of suspension travel — and the wheel sizes confirm this is built with genuine off-road intent, not just the appearance of it. Kerb weight is reported to be around 204 kilograms (approximately 450 pounds), placing it neatly between the F 450 GS and F 900 GS on the scales as well as in the lineup. The headlight already shows a finished X-shaped design borrowed from the R 1300 GS, though the characteristic GS beak is absent — likely a sign that front-end bodywork is still in progress. The overall proportions draw comparisons to the Yamaha Ténéré 700, which is no accident: both the Ténéré 700 and the Honda XL750 Transalp are reportedly being used as development benchmarks during testing. The powertrain is where things get genuinely complicated. The engine is a parallel twin with clear ties to the F 450 GS platform, but how heavily BMW reworks it — or whether it builds something new entirely — remains open. The most concrete reference point is the Norton Atlas, where BMW partner TVS uses a 585cc version of a reworked parallel twin producing 70 hp. That engine is regarded as a plausible starting point, though the prototype's motor differs from the Norton unit in several visible areas. There's also a technical wrinkle worth noting: the F 450 GS runs an unusual 135-degree crankpin offset, while the Norton twin uses the more conventional 270-degree firing interval common in this class. That difference affects how the engine feels under throttle and how well power can be metered on loose surfaces — exactly the conditions this bike is being built for. Whether BMW carries its unconventional setup into the middleweight or switches to the standard layout is one of the more interesting unanswered questions surrounding the project. Power output is expected to land somewhere in the 65–80 hp range, keeping it well clear of the F 900 GS's 105 hp. The middleweight adventure segment has changed dramatically since the original F 650 GS era. The Yamaha Ténéré 700 and KTM 690 Adventure have set a high bar for off-road performance at accessible price points, while the Royal Enfield Himalayan and Honda NX500 have pushed the entry point lower still. It's a crowded, competitive space — and it's one BMW has been absent from for long enough that the Ténéré 700 and Transalp have had time to build loyal followings. A new middleweight GS, priced between the F 450 GS and F 900 GS, would give BMW a genuine answer to all of them. One estimate places the India price around 1.2 million rupees (roughly $12,500 USD), though that figure carries no manufacturer backing. What's clear is that BMW's intent is to compete on capability first — the 21-inch front wheel, long-travel suspension, and F 900 GS-derived braking all point to a machine that takes off-road performance seriously rather than treating it as a styling exercise. A production launch is not expected before 2028, and the unfinished state of the prototype confirms there's significant development work still ahead. EICMA 2026 is the earliest realistic opportunity for an official reveal, though even that isn't confirmed. For riders shopping the middleweight segment right now, the prototype is a signal worth paying attention to — BMW is coming, and it's building something that looks like it means business.
